prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- German zookeepers in Nuremberg will bottle-feed a four-week-old polar bear and rear it away from its mother after concerns the mother would eat her cub, officials said Thursday. Zookeepers fear the unnamed polar bear cub could be at risk of being eaten. The cub, which doesn't yet have a name, was being cared for at Nuremberg City Zoo, where it was resting under heat lamps and is drinking formula. "It's gaining weight, it's very hungry, it drinks a lot of milk," said Alexandra Foghammar, a spokeswoman for the city. The zoo announced Thursday that the cub is female. Wednesday, the zoo said keepers decided to take the cub away from its mother, Vera, because the mother was showing signs of being upset and confused, taking her baby in and out of the animals' enclosure. "We were 100 percent sure that the baby was going to die if we didn't take it away from her," Nuremberg zoo director Dag Encke told Time magazine. "This would have been a death verdict for the cub." The zoo confirmed earlier this week that its other female polar bear, Vilma, had eaten her two offspring. The zoo said it feared Vera would do the same, so it took her cub away as a precaution. Since then, the cub is thriving in the care of humans, but Vera seems to miss her cub, Foghammar said.  Watch how zoo has faced criticism over polar bears. » . "The mother is a little bit nervous," she said. "She walks around and is searching for the baby, but the responsible persons for the zoo say this is normal. It will continue for three or four days. It's a normal situation." The zookeepers are pondering whether to bring another adult bear, possibly the cub's father, Felix, to the zoo to help Vera overcome her loss, and are seeking another small bear to serve as a companion for the rescued cub, Time reported. The zoo said a keeper entered Vilma's enclosure Monday and noticed that her two cubs were nowhere to be found. The zoo said it assumes Vilma ate her young because she believed the cubs were sick, though zookeepers say the cubs were last seen on Sunday and appeared in good health. But Foghammar told Time that the separation of the bears was bad for the "principle of wildlife conservation" at the zoo: "Now the cub will not grow up to act in a natural way, just as the mother lacked the experience to bring up a cub." The plight of the cub follows the case last year of Knut, a cub rejected by its mother at Berlin Zoo who became the focus of a media frenzy after animal rights campaigners called for it to be killed, claiming it had become too dependent on humans. outputs.L1:
(CNN) — German zookeepers in Nuremberg will bottle-feed a four-week-old polar bear cub and raise it apart from its mother amid concerns that she might eat her offspring, officials said Thursday.

Zookeepers feared the unnamed cub could be at risk of being eaten. The cub, which does not yet have a name, is being cared for at Nuremberg City Zoo, where it is resting under heat lamps and drinking formula.

“It’s gaining weight, it’s very hungry, it drinks a lot of milk,” said Alexandra Foghammar, a spokeswoman for the city.

The zoo announced Thursday that the cub is female.

On Wednesday, the zoo said keepers had decided to separate the cub from its mother, Vera, because Vera was showing signs of distress and confusion, repeatedly carrying her baby in and out of the animals’ enclosure.

“We were 100 percent sure that the baby was going to die if we didn’t take it away from her,” Nuremberg zoo director Dag Encke told Time magazine. “This would have been a death verdict for the cub.”

Earlier this week, the zoo confirmed that its other female polar bear, Vilma, had eaten her two offspring. Officials said they feared Vera might do the same, and therefore removed her cub as a precaution.

Since then, the cub has been thriving under human care, though Vera appears to miss her offspring, Foghammar said.

“The mother is a little bit nervous,” she said. “She walks around and is searching for the baby, but the responsible persons for the zoo say this is normal. It will continue for three or four days. It’s a normal situation.”

The zookeepers are considering bringing another adult bear—possibly the cub’s father, Felix—to the zoo to help Vera cope with her loss. They are also seeking another small bear to serve as a companion for the rescued cub, Time reported.

The zoo said a keeper entered Vilma’s enclosure Monday and noticed that her two cubs were missing. Officials said they assume Vilma ate her young because she believed they were sick, although zookeepers said the cubs had last been seen Sunday and appeared to be in good health.

However, Foghammar told Time that separating the bears was detrimental to the zoo’s “principle of wildlife conservation.”

“Now the cub will not grow up to act in a natural way, just as the mother lacked the experience to bring up a cub,” she said.

The cub’s plight follows last year’s case of Knut, a cub rejected by its mother at Berlin Zoo. Knut became the focus of intense media attention after animal-rights campaigners called for him to be killed, arguing that he had become too dependent on humans.

The cub, born to a polar bear named Vera, was taken into human care after zoo staff observed what they described as increasingly troubling behavior. Officials said Vera had been carrying the cub around in her mouth and appeared agitated, raising fears that the infant’s life could be in danger.

Zoo officials said the decision to separate the cub from her mother was not taken lightly, but that the animal’s survival had to come first.

“The cub is now being cared for around the clock,” the zoo said, adding that keepers and veterinarians were feeding her by hand and monitoring her condition closely.

The tiny bear’s rescue immediately drew comparisons to **Knut**, the Berlin Zoo polar bear who became an international celebrity after he was rejected by his mother in 2006 and raised by zookeepers. Knut’s story captivated Germany and turned him into a media sensation, drawing huge crowds and sparking debate over hand-rearing wild animals.

Nuremberg Zoo officials said they were aware of the public interest but stressed that the cub’s welfare was their priority.

“For now, the most important thing is that she eats, gains weight and stays healthy,” officials said.

The female cub has not yet been put on public display. Zoo staff said she will remain behind the scenes while she is stabilized and cared for by specialists.

Polar bear mothers in captivity can sometimes reject or injure their cubs, especially if they are stressed or inexperienced. In rare cases, zoo officials say, mothers may kill or consume their young.

The Nuremberg cub’s case is expected to draw significant attention in Germany, where Knut’s hand-rearing made him one of the country’s most famous animals. But zoo officials cautioned that every case is different — and that the cub’s first weeks remain critical.
